question: How do you summarise a sample (mean, variance, histogram, PMF) and explore it for outliers and group differences, using NSFG pregnancy lengths of first babies versus others?
contributions: Defines mean vs average, variance, standard deviation, histogram, PMF, mode, outlier, trimming, bins, relative risk, conditional probability
Worked NSFG example: do first babies arrive late?

results.claim: A mean can mislead when there is no typical value: pumpkins of 1, 1, 1, 3, 3 and 591 pounds have mean 100 pounds.
results.setup: Six pumpkins: three decorative at 1 lb, two pie at 3 lb, one Atlantic Giant at 591 lb
results.quote: The mean of this sample is 100

results.claim: Relative risk of a first baby being early is 1.08 (18.2% vs 16.8% for others), about 8% more likely.
results.setup: NSFG pregnancy lengths; early = born in Week 37 or earlier; first babies vs others
results.quote: For other babies it is 16.8%, so the relative risk is 1.08.

limits: Significance of the first-baby effect is not tested here; the chapter says 'let's assume that these effects are real' and defers sample variance (n-1) to Chapter 8.
NSFG sample sizes, the dataset size and the 18.2%/16.8% derivation are not given in this chapter (Chapter 1 and exercises).
Code is Python 2 (print statements) with custom Pmf.py, myplot.py, thinkstats.py; dated.
No stated rule for trimming outliers; values between 20 and 30 weeks are 'hard to interpret'.
practices: Distinguish the mean (a formula) from an average (any measure of central tendency); do not report a mean when there is no typical value (Sec 2.1).
Report standard deviation rather than variance, since its units match the data (Sec 2.2).
Look at the distribution, not only summary statistics, which obscure the data (Sec 2.3).
Compare groups of different size with PMFs rather than histograms, to remove sample-size effects (Sec 2.5-2.7).
Use bar plots for PMFs with few values and line plots for many smooth values (Sec 2.7).
Always check for outliers; they may be errors or real, and trimming is sometimes appropriate (Sec 2.8).
After exploring, zoom in on the region of difference and plot the PMF difference in percentage points (Sec 2.9).
Summarise group differences with relative risk after binning into early/on time/late (Sec 2.10).
Use conditional probability for questions asked given what is already known, by dropping values and renormalising (Sec 2.11).
Choose reported statistics for the audience and goal: emphasise differences vs give context (Sec 2.12).
